item.title: Splitting Planar Necklaces with Few Straight Cuts
item.description: arXiv:2610.27956v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In the classical necklace splitting problem, beads of different colors lie on a line, and the goal is to divide them among $k$ agents using as few cuts as possible so that every agent receives the same number of beads of each color. We study the planar analog in which a cut is a full straight line and the objective is minimizing the number of lines: $m$ points colored red and blue must be separated by straight-line cuts into regions that can be allocated to $k$ agents so that each agent receives the same number of points of each color. Projection to a line gives $2(k-1)$ cuts, and $k-1$ are sometimes necessary; we give algorithms, static and dynamic, that provably close part of this gap. We develop several approaches that capitalize on the extra degree of freedom: a ``star'' search that produces solutions with as few as $\lceil \frac{k}{2} \rceil$ cuts and never more than $k$ whenever a fair contiguous circular partition exists, with further guarantees for evenly spaced input, and a general algorithm that produces at most $k + \log_2(k+1) - 2$ cuts in $\Theta(m \log k)$ time, built on a one-dimensional necklace splitting subroutine that requires no presorting. We then adapt the general algorithm to a dynamic setting, maintaining exact fairness and the cut bound under arbitrary relocation of points, with expected update time that scales with the total distance moved.
item.dc:creator: Rishi Advani, Abolfazl Asudeh

item.title: Estimating the intrinsic error of 3D point clouds acquisition techniques: A comparative study on instruments of the violin family
item.description: arXiv:2610.28098v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This study compares ten digital 3D acquisition techniques applied to violin family instrument plates, assessing their accuracy and relevance for scientific and cultural heritage applications. Evaluated methods include two photogrammetric workflows, medical and industrial computed tomography, terrestrial laser scanning, two structured-light configurations (blue light and infrared), and three consumer-grade iPad Pro approaches: TrueDepth scanning and LiDAR using two different applications. The methods were applied to five historical instruments from the "Musical Instruments Museum" (Brussels) and the "Mus\'ee de la Musique" (Paris). Since no geometric ground truth is available, accuracy is assessed through systematic pairwise point-to-plane comparisons of the resulting point clouds. These comparisons are jointly analysed to estimate the intrinsic error of each technique (i.e. the expected discrepancy between the model and the true but unknown geometry) without designating any technique as reference. Results are discussed with respect to intended uses, offering recommendations for techniques depending on the dedicated objectives.
item.dc:creator: Phil\'emon Beghin, Jean-Philippe \'Echard, Anthony Peeters, Arnaud Schenkel, Anne-Emmanuelle Ceulemans, Fran\c{c}ois Glineur

item.title: A Bochner Weitzenb\"ock Decomposition for Cellular Sheaf Laplacians, Curvature and Neural Sheaf Diffusion
item.description: arXiv:2610.28455v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We extend the Bochner-Weitzenb\"ock decomposition to cellular sheaf Laplacians, splitting it into a positive semidefinite term, the Bochner sheaf Laplacian, and a block diagonal term, the Forman curvature. We show that the Bochner Laplacians form a class of cellular sheaves that extends both connection and matrix-weighted Laplacians, and generalizes signed graphs to $d$ dimensions. We give a holonomy characterization of their kernel, prove the related Cheeger inequalities, and attach to them a random walk that generalizes the Gremban expansion. For the Forman term, we prove a discrete Bochner theorem, which bounds the first cohomology of a cellular sheaf with nonnegative curvature, and we read the whole decomposition as an opinion-dynamics model. We then apply this machinery to Sheaf Neural Networks, whose learnt Laplacian is otherwise unobserved. The Bochner interpretation yields a node-level conviction score that acts as an operational importance measure under frozen-model interventions, while the Forman profile provides a local descriptor of the learnt operator.
item.dc:creator: Francesco Maria Guadagnuolo, Alessio Borgi, Dorina Thanou, Pietro Li\`o

item.title: CyberHull: Deterministic Malicious URL Isolation via Convex Hull
item.description: arXiv:2610.27675v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The emergence of increasingly sophisticated and evasion-resistant phishing attack strategies represents a significant threat to modern cybersecurity, particularly in cyber-physical systems and internet-based networks. Traditional probabilistic methods and certain machine learning approaches often struggle to detect novel attacks and may lack interpretability or portability. To address these challenges, we introduce CyberHull, a resource-efficient and deterministic framework for identifying malicious URLs through mathematically defined convex hull boundaries across multiple orthogonal feature domains, including structural content entropy, hyperlink graph topology, and semantic token distribution. CyberHull constructs compact convex hulls, referred to as vaults, using the QuickHull algorithm, with a training complexity of O(n log n) under suitable assumptions. URL classification is performed through point-in-polyhedron tests that impose relatively low computational overhead on standard CPUs. Experimental results demonstrate that CyberHull achieves 92 percent detection accuracy, substantially outperforming a baseline linear approach based on Principal Component Analysis (PCA), which achieves 32 percent accuracy. Furthermore, CyberHull offers a computationally efficient alternative to resource-intensive deep learning approaches for malicious URL detection.
item.dc:creator: Avijit Gayen, Aniket Ghosal, Durba Chakraborty, Sayan Mondal, Md Abdul Aziz Al Aman, Angshuman Jana

item.title: Logarithmic edge-length ratios for planar drawings of 2-trees
item.description: arXiv:2610.28030v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: For a planar graph $G$ with at least one edge, let $\rho(G)$ be the infimum of the ratio of the longest to the shortest edge length over all planar straight-line drawings of $G$. We prove that every $n$-vertex $2$-tree $G$ satisfies $\rho(G)\le4+5\lfloor\log_2(2n-3)\rfloor$. This improves the known $O(\sqrt n)$ upper bound and, together with the lower bound of Bla\v{z}ej, Fiala and Liotta, shows that the maximum of $\rho(G)$ over $n$-vertex $2$-trees is $\Theta(\log n)$. The proof adapts Biedl's recursive bar construction using nonintegral heights and applies a height-preserving straightening theorem.
item.dc:creator: Zahra Sabaei, Yasmin Tousinejad, Fatemeh Emami

item.title: Two $\operatorname{ReLU}$ Layers is All You Need
item.description: arXiv:2610.28587v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We prove that every $\operatorname{ReLU}$ network can be exactly simulated by a $\operatorname{ReLU}$ network with two hidden layers. We present two proofs: one that is based on fillings in homological algebra and a direct combinatorial proof.
item.dc:creator: Florestan Brunck, Christoph Hertrich, Kilian Ruess, Jack Stade, Amir Yehudayoff

item.title: FPTAS for Polygonal Multi-Robot Motion Planning
item.description: arXiv:2610.20244v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study multi-robot motion planning in a polygonal environment with polygonal robots. The setting of the problem consists of a polygonal domain $\mathcal{W}$ with $n$ vertices and $k$ robots $R_1,\dots,R_k$ translating in $\mathcal{W}$ each of which is represented by a polygon of constant complexity. Given a source configuration $\mathbf{s}$ and a target configuration $\mathbf{t}$ of the robots in $\mathcal{W}$, the goal of the problem is to find a collision-free motion plan from $\mathbf{s}$ to $\mathbf{t}$ that is shortest with respect to some cost function. We present the first fully polynomial-time approximation schemes (FPTAS) for motion planning with any fixed number $k$ of robots, under the min-sum objective, the min-max objective, and the min-makespan objective. Here, the min-sum variant aims to minimize the total traveling distance of all robots, the min-max variant aims to minimize the maximum traveling distance of a single robot, and the min-makespan variant aims to minimize the total time cost under the assumption that all robots move with a maximum speed $1$. The algorithm directly generalizes to the problem in any fixed dimension $d$, with a polytope environment and polytope robots. Our result settles an open question of Agarwal, Halperin, Sharir, Steiger [SODA'24] and Agarwal, Holmgren, Steiger [SODA'26], who gave an FPTAS for $k=2$ unit-square robots and a bicriteria-approximation algorithm for a fixed number $k$ of unit-square or unit-disk robots, respectively. Compared to the previous results, our algorithm is substantially simpler.
item.dc:creator: Sayan Bandyapadhyay, William Lochet, Saket Saurabh, Jie Xue
